summary: Europe names its Ukraine-talks team as Trump, Xi and Putin plan to meet; Trump says he needs no Iran deal; Congress summons Nvidia's ex-CEO; COP31 splits over fossil fuels.

question.text: Several stories today are about who gets a seat at the table: Europe in Ukraine talks, Congress over chip exports, poorer countries at COP31. When a new party joins a negotiation, what else might change besides its own influence, for better or worse?

read.title: How Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia impacts China's AI supply chain
read.summary: How much of China's AI computing still depends on Nvidia, how fast Huawei is catching up, and what the Huang scandal could change.

topics.heading: Europe picks a five-country team for Ukraine talks; Trump, Xi and Putin plan to meet
topics.summary: At an informal summit in Dublin, EU leaders agreed that the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, with EU institutions, will speak for Europe at the next round of US-led Ukraine talks.[^1][^2] The White House says Trump, Xi and Putin plan a first three-way meeting at next week's APEC summit in Shenzhen.[^4]

lead.title: EU leaders bring Italy and Poland into Ukraine peace talks team as Kallas fights for spot

alsoReported.title: Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice
Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China

article: European Union leaders meeting informally in Dublin on Friday agreed on a team for the next round of US-brokered talks on ending Russia's war in Ukraine. Europe will be represented by the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, together with the EU's institutions, rather than by a single envoy.[^1][^2] European Council President António Costa said it was essential "to speak with only one voice" and that only Ukraine can decide matters of its own territory.[^2] Ukraine's President Zelensky, who met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner near Dublin after their talks with Putin, said Europeans "will have a voice" in the next round.[^6]

Some background: the latest round of US-led talks, in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10-11, produced agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange but no breakthrough.[^23] Russia still demands all of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine, which Kyiv refuses.[^24] Europe pays a large share of Ukraine's costs and fears a deal made over its head; RTÉ reports Ukraine faces a funding gap of about €70 billion in 2027.[^2]

The choice was not smooth. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wanted one envoy, and EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas sought a role but was not backed.[^1] Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov mocked the Europeans as squabbling "like spiders in a jar", while Kushner said Europe must be at the table for any deal to be completed.[^3] No date has been set for the next round.[^3]

Separately, the White House says Trump, Xi Jinping and Putin plan to meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, next week, the first such three-way meeting. US officials say the focus is nuclear arms control, since the last US-Russia arms treaty, New START, lapsed in February, and the Iran war; they do not expect an agreement.[^4][^5] Zelensky has voiced concern that Ukraine could be discussed without Kyiv, and the Kremlin rejects comparisons with the 1945 Yalta conference, where great powers divided Europe.[^5] My read: the things to watch are whether Europe's team actually gets into the room, and whether Shenzhen stays on arms control.
topics.differences: US officials say Ukraine is not the focus of the Shenzhen meeting;[^4] a Kremlin aide said this week that Putin would continue Ukraine talks with Trump at APEC.[^24] The Kremlin says Europe must first show it is "ready" to help the peace process.[^1]

topics.heading: Trump says the US doesn't need an Iran deal; Iran and the US dispute a strike in Bahrain
topics.summary: Trump said "we don't need a deal with Iran" and took Vice-President Vance off the talks.[^7] On Friday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they hit a US radar in Bahrain; US Central Command says it shot down two drones and nothing was damaged.[^8]

lead.title: Trump says deal with Iran not needed, pulls Vance off negotiations

alsoReported.title: Iran says it hit US radar station in Bahrain, diplomats scramble to avert war
UN nuclear watchdog urges Iran to take 'steps' towards inspections

article: President Trump wrote on Thursday that "we don't need a deal with Iran" and moved Vice-President JD Vance off the peace effort.[^7] He argues that the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions are working, saying Iran "militarily, is effectively over."[^7] In a radio interview he said he would strike again if things went "the other way."[^10] Iranian officials, for their part, deny reports of a recent US-Iran meeting in Qatar, the main go-between.[^25]

Fighting at sea continues. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that they targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for a US strike on a telecom tower in southern Iran, and that a gas tanker hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz.[^8][^10] US Central Command says two attack drones launched toward Bahrain were shot down with no damage, and the tanker claim has not been independently confirmed.[^8] Yemen's Houthis, allied with Iran, claim attacks on Saudi oil sites, including the pipeline Saudi Arabia uses to send oil around Hormuz; Saudi statements mention only interceptions.[^11]

The nuclear question is also open. A confidential report by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN nuclear watchdog, says it cannot conclude that Iran has not diverted declared nuclear material, and that it does not know the location or status of an enrichment plant at Isfahan. Its board will discuss the report next week, and Iran says monitoring talks cannot go ahead while it faces military threats.[^9]

Oil prices barely moved: Brent crude settled at $95.84 a barrel on Friday, about 2.5% lower for the week.[^22] My read: with Washington saying it can wait and Tehran in no hurry to reopen the strait on US terms, the likeliest path is a slow, costly standoff, with the risk that a single disputed incident escalates quickly.
topics.differences: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say their strike hit a US radar in Bahrain; US Central Command says only drones were launched and all were shot down.[^8] The Houthis say they hit Saudi oil facilities; Saudi and coalition statements report only interceptions.[^11]

topics.heading: 53 countries and groups urge Israel to let more winter supplies into Gaza
topics.summary: A statement led by the UK, Qatar and Jordan asks Israel to let in shelter, fuel and health supplies before winter.[^12] Israel says more than 93,000 tents have entered and blames Hamas; Gaza's Civil Defence says a baby died of cold in a tent.[^12][^13]

lead.title: Dozens of nations, organizations demand Israel let more winter supplies into Gaza

alsoReported.title: Palestinian baby dies from cold in Gaza amid Israeli restrictions on aid

article: On Friday, 53 countries and organisations, led by the UK, Qatar and Jordan, called on Israel to immediately allow shelter materials, fuel, water, sanitation and health supplies into Gaza, warning of hypothermia and lung infections as winter arrives.[^12] UN figures cited in the coverage say about 65% of Gazans live in tents or temporary shelters, and the WHO reports 33,000 more acute respiratory infections than a year earlier.[^12]

Gaza's Civil Defence said a nine-month-old baby died of the cold in a tent in Khan Younis, and that five people died when an embankment collapsed onto tents after flooding.[^13] Israel's aid agency COGAT says more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks of winter supplies have entered. Israel says the criticism distracts from Hamas's responsibility, keeps limits on "dual-use" items (goods it says could also serve military purposes), and says rebuilding will not start until Hamas disarms.[^12]

Gaza has been under a US-brokered ceasefire since October 2025, overseen by a US-led Board of Peace. The truce has stopped large-scale fighting but not all violence: the Israeli army says it killed more than ten militants this week for violating the ceasefire.[^10]

Israeli politics will shape what comes next. After the Oct 27 election, Gadi Eisenkot has the first chance to form a government, but his bloc holds 48 of the 61 seats needed. Israel's Channel 12 reports he now prefers talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties over the Arab-led parties, while caretaker Prime Minister Netanyahu is lobbying the same parties' rabbis.[^26][^27] My read: major decisions on Gaza's next phase are unlikely before a new government is formed.
topics.differences: Israel says it has let in more than 93,000 tents and that Hamas is responsible for the situation; the 53 signatories, UN officials and the US-led Board of Peace say supplies are not enough.[^12]

topics.heading: Congress summons ex-Nvidia CEO Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick over chips to China
topics.summary: The Senate Banking Committee asked Jensen Huang to testify on Dec 3 and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Dec 10, or face subpoenas, over how restricted AI chips reached China.[^15] Nvidia's market value fell below $4 trillion.[^14]

lead.title: Senate Banking Committee asks Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify over 'significant national security concerns' next month, or face subpoenas

alsoReported.title: US Senate summons Nvidia's Huang, Lutnick to testify
China warns US over chip curbs as suspected spy's firm got banned chips

article: A day after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, Congress moved to question him. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott asked Huang to testify on Dec 3 and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Dec 10, or face subpoenas, citing "significant national security concerns."[^15] Three House committees want Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer on Dec 1-2.[^14] President Trump says the FBI is investigating, and Nvidia's board has started an independent review.[^15]

The issue is export controls: US rules that ban selling the most advanced AI chips to China. Huang resigned after admitting affairs, one reportedly with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore data-centre company and Nvidia partner that US authorities are investigating over alleged chip smuggling. US officials suspect she worked for Chinese intelligence, which China denies.[^14][^16] Bloomberg, cited by Euronews, reports that a Shanghai company she founded obtained servers with Nvidia H800 chips, which have been banned for export to China since 2023.[^16]

Reactions cross party lines. Trump called Huang "honourable"; Republican Senator Jim Banks says Lutnick defied Trump's own line on selling top chips to China, and Democrat Elizabeth Warren wants loopholes closed.[^14][^15] House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks of a "developing consensus" for tighter limits, and China's foreign ministry warned the US against "abuse of export control measures."[^16] Nvidia's market value is now below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025.[^14]

Why it matters: Nvidia's chips power most large AI systems, and the scandal lands as China builds its own. Rest of World, citing IDC data, says Huawei shipped 28% of the AI chips sold in China in the first half of 2026, against Nvidia's 34%.[^21] My read: stricter export rules now look more likely, which could speed up China's push to rely on its own chips. Nvidia's quarterly results on Nov 17 will be the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.[^28]
topics.differences: US officials, cited anonymously, link Huang's former partner to Chinese intelligence; China denies it and warns the US against abusing export controls.[^16] Trump defends Huang as honourable, while senators in both parties question how chips reached China.[^14][^15]

topics.heading: COP31 hosts publish a menu of options as negotiators split over fossil fuels
topics.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, the summit's leaders issued a list of ideas for its final decision, from faster electrification to money for adaptation.[^17] Arab states, India and others resist firm fossil-fuel language; a first draft is due early next week.[^17][^18]

lead.title: COP31 Bulletin Day 5: Cover decision wishlist issued as China bows out of COP33

alsoReported.title: UN chief urges drastic emissions cuts as COP31 wrestles with fossil fuels

article: COP31, this year's UN climate conference, is being held in Antalya, Turkey, with Turkey and Australia sharing the presidency, and is due to end on Nov 20. On Friday the presidencies published a "summary of reflections": a menu of possible items for the summit's main decision text, which they stress is not a draft and has not been agreed.[^17]

The ideas include welcoming a goal to raise electricity's share of final energy use from about 20% to 35% by 2035, limiting how far warming overshoots 1.5C, more money to help countries adapt to climate change, cutting methane leaks, and phasing out "unilateral climate trade measures", widely read as a reference to the EU's carbon border tax.[^17] Countries had until Saturday to send written views, and a first draft is expected early next week.[^18]

The divisions are familiar. Arab states object to mentioning last year's COP30 roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, and Saudi Arabia questioned a UN report on overshoot because it was not peer-reviewed.[^17] India and the G77 group of developing countries reject firm targets or language naming specific fuels, while the EU says electrification must run on clean energy and Brazil wants clearer roadmaps.[^17][^18] UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in emissions; the United States is absent for a second year.[^18]

Also from the talks: China has ruled itself out of hosting COP33 in 2028, and a Pacific fund for climate resilience is $300 million short of its 2026 target.[^17] My read: the realistic test of COP31 is whether the final text keeps any concrete commitment on fossil fuels, more than how ambitious it sounds.
topics.differences: Arab states oppose naming the COP30 fossil-fuel roadmap, and India and the G77 reject fuel-specific targets, while the EU and Brazil push for clean-energy and roadmap language.[^17][^18]

topics.heading: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases as armed attacks slow the response
topics.summary: Congo's government reports 11,042 confirmed Ebola cases and at least 5,387 deaths, the second-largest outbreak on record.[^19] The UN says attacks by armed groups, including one that killed 66 civilians, are holding back the response.[^20]

lead.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak: Unrest fuelled by armed groups holds back response

alsoReported.title: Ebola cases in DR Congo pass 11,000, with 5,387 deaths

article: The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak has passed 11,000 confirmed cases. Government data show 11,042 cases and at least 5,387 deaths across eight of the country's 26 provinces, with cases also reported elsewhere in East, Central and West Africa.[^19] Only the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic, with more than 28,600 cases, was larger.[^19]

This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer type of Ebola that kills about half of those infected and has no approved vaccine or treatment.[^19] The World Health Organization approved trials of two new vaccines earlier this month, with results expected in early 2027.[^19]

The UN says violence is making the work harder. It reports about 400 to 500 new cases a week, with the virus moving from towns in Ituri province into rural areas, and an attack by the ADF armed group in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians, including three health workers, while health facilities were looted.[^20] Many deaths happen outside treatment centres, which makes it harder to trace people who were exposed.[^19]

Why it matters: Ebola spreads through close contact, so stopping it depends on trust, safe burials and access to communities, all hard in a conflict zone. My read: the outbreak is also a test of how quickly new vaccines can be developed and delivered for a rare strain.
